  visited at all, so collection cost is proportional to live
   data rather than heap size, and compaction — zero
  fragmentation, perfectly cache-friendly allocation — falls
   out for free. The bill is memory: half the heap is always
   reserved, and long-lived objects get copied on every
  pass.

  The 1970s turned to the pause problem. Baker's incremental
   collector (1978) interleaved small collection steps with
  program execution using read barriers; Dijkstra's
  on-the-fly collector (1978) established the tri-color
  abstraction — white, gray, black — that still frames every
   concurrent collector, and Steele explored multiprocessing
   collection even earlier. These designs were delicate, but
   they proved the crucial point: a collector's work can
  overlap with the program's.

  Then came the idea that made GC commercially boring in the
   best way: generations. Lieberman and Hewitt (1983)
  formalized the weak generational hypothesis — most objects
   die young — and David Ungar (1984) built it into
  Smalltalk as generation scavenging. New objects live in a
  small nursery collected cheaply and often; survivors are
  promoted to an old generation collected rarely. Write
  barriers and remembered sets track the rare old-to-young
  pointers. Because it matched actual allocation behavior,
  collection became fast in practice, not just in theory.

  Mainstream adoption followed. Java shipped generational
  collectors in 1996, then grew a zoo: parallel throughput
  collectors, the mostly-concurrent CMS in the early 2000s,
  and G1, which sliced the heap into regions and collected
  the least-valuable ones first to honor a pause goal
  (default from JDK 9). .

 ○ Evaluating…  1.1k
